artworks.title: Ixion
artworks.description: Ribera's Prado canvas binds the Lapith king to the wheel that never stops: a tormentor turns the rim while Ixion's body twists in tenebrist shadow — one of the surviving Furias of eternal insolence against Zeus.

artworks.title: Ixion, King of the Lapiths, Deceived by Juno
artworks.description: Rubens stages the crime before the wheel: Ixion embraces the cloud-form of Juno while Zeus looks on — desire for the queen of heaven that will birth the Centaurs and earn the spinning punishment.

artworks.title: Ixion (from The Four Disgracers)
artworks.artist: Hendrick Goltzius, after Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem
artworks.description: Goltzius engraves Cornelis' foreshortened fall: Ixion plummets through air toward the wheel below — one of the Four Disgracers who insulted the gods and learned the measure of Tartarus.

artworks.title: The Torture of Ixion
artworks.description: Langetti's Venetian tenebrism locks the king to the fiery wheel — muscle and flame in the dark, the Lapith's eternal spin rendered as raw underworld theatre.

popCulture.title: Ixion
popCulture.description: The Lapith king's fiery wheel remains the emblem of eternal spinning punishment — desire bound to a circle that never stops.

popCulture.title: 28978 Ixion
popCulture.description: A large Kuiper-belt object took Ixion's name — the wheel-bound king carried into the outer solar system.

popCulture.title: Centaur
popCulture.description: Greek tradition makes Ixion father of the Centaurs by the cloud-form Nephele — the wheel-bound Lapith as the genealogical source of the horse-men.
